analysis.one_liner: Pauses the legal clock for workers' unpaid-wage lawsuits during federal wage investigations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either chamber and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When the Labor Department opens an investigation into an employer over unpaid minimum wage or overtime, the bill would pause the two-year time limit workers have to sue for back pay until the investigation ends. Without the pause, investigations that drag on can let the legal deadline expire while evidence is being gathered, leaving workers unable to recover wages they were owed.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers underpaid them on minimum wage or overtime. Their lawsuits would not expire while a federal investigation is underway, preserving their ability to recover back wages and liquidated damages in court if the agency process does not fully make them whole.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers owed unpaid minimum wage or overtime

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Portal-to-Portal Act so that the statute of limitations for unpaid minimum wage, unpaid overtime, and liquidated damages claims is tolled from the day the Secretary of Labor notifies an employer of an investigation until the day the employer is notified the investigation concluded [S2][S3].

This matters because a federal wage investigation can take longer than the two-year limitations period in the Fair Labor Standards Act; without a pause, an employer under investigation can effectively run out the clock and escape private lawsuits for older violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing wage-and-hour claims would bear longer exposure to lawsuits and potentially larger back-pay awards, since older violations would remain recoverable for the duration of any investigation.

drawbacks.text: Extending the limitations period increases employers' legal exposure and litigation costs, which larger companies treat as a compliance risk; that is the strongest good-faith objection to the bill, though it is the cost the bill is designed to impose on violators [S3].

The bill is narrow: it only pauses the clock during Labor Department investigations and does not by itself recover a single dollar of unpaid wages or strengthen enforcement staff or penalties [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give workers a fair chance to use the courts for wage violations the government is already investigating, at a real but targeted cost to employers who underpay. Its main weakness is modesty: it is a procedural fix for one gap in wage enforcement, not a broad anti-wage-theft measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to two House committees, then sent to a subcommittee, and no committee ever reported it back for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the Wage Theft Prevention Act on July 23, 2009, joined by Reps. Lynn Woolsey and Phil Hare as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On October 22, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last action ever taken on it [S5].

It drew 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Senate companion ever advanced; the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing potential wage-and-hour lawsuits are better off, because the limitations clock for unpaid wages was never paused and older violations remain harder to sue over. Wage enforcement stayed as it was, with lawsuits expiring while federal investigations continue.

sides.party_line_note: All 4 cosponsors were House Democrats with no Republican support, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers with unpaid-wage exposure (staffing, restaurants, retail, construction subcontractors)
industries.note: The bill would have extended how long workers could sue them for unpaid minimum wage and overtime whenever the Labor Department was investigating. Its cost falls on violators, while its benefit goes to workers recovering back pay.
